strengths: The paper addresses an important and longstanding question: why distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL. The proposed loss-decomposition perspective is creative, and the basic cross-entropy decomposition is intuitive under the stated validity condition.

The manuscript is generally well organized, provides useful intuition and figures, relates the proposal to C51, Neural FQI/FZI, and maximum-entropy RL, and appropriately acknowledges that the main analysis is specific to categorical distributional RL.

The empirical study has reasonable breadth, covering Atari and continuous-control environments, categorical and quantile critics, multiple atom counts, and several ablations. Learning curves include variability over three Atari seeds and five MuJoCo seeds.
The appendices make a substantial effort to expose proofs, implementation choices, and limitations. The work raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The central inference is unsupported. Proposition 2 decomposes a critic-fitting loss, but ordinary C51 or distributional SAC does not make its policy maximize the resulting cross-entropy term. Section 5 instead defines a new Bellman operator that explicitly inserts an arbitrary increasing function of this term as a reward bonus. No equivalence between that invented DERPI objective and the evaluated CDRL algorithms is established. Moreover, the convergence discussion assumes fixed q_theta, whereas q_theta changes throughout actual distributional learning.

Cross-entropy is incorrectly treated as a discrepancy: H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q), so across state-action pairs it conflates target entropy with estimation mismatch and depends on the discretization. Likewise, mu is not formally a higher-moment-only residual; it can carry first-moment information, while the single-bin component records only a coarse mean bin rather than the mean itself. The decomposition is also non-unique because epsilon is arbitrary, weakening the claim that this is an intrinsic regularizer.

The key ablation does not isolate the claimed regularization. H(mu,q) replaces the original target p by mu and discards the mean-related term. As the experimental epsilon decreases, the construction removes mass from the mean-containing bin and rescales the remaining bins; it does not approach a mean-only DQN target and can change the target expectation. Consequently, degradation toward DQN-level returns may simply reflect increasingly distorted critic targets, not removal of uncertainty-aware exploration.

Several formal statements or proofs are incorrect. Equation 39 establishes at most O(Delta), not o(Delta). The appendix invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem after proving only KL non-expansiveness with factor one. Proposition 3 blurs finite-Delta probability statements with weak convergence to a Dirac distribution. The DERPI proof drops the bonus in its optimality comparison, contains inconsistent state-action indices, and does not resolve the policy dependence of the target return distribution. These are substantive issues rather than cosmetic proof gaps.

The experiments report only return curves and never measure the asserted mechanism through visitation, target-current divergence, calibrated environmental uncertainty, or exploration efficiency. The Atari evaluation uses eight selected games and three seeds without aggregate scores or statistical comparisons; several MuJoCo interpolation trends are weak or non-monotone. Performance interactions among AC, SAC, DAC, and DSAC do not by themselves demonstrate distinct exploration directions and could arise from critic optimization or stability differences.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the empirical claims. No code is supplied, despite the checklist answering that open access is provided and then stating that code will only be released after acceptance. Important details such as Atari hyperparameters and preprocessing, categorical support ranges, complete architectures, evaluation protocols, hyperparameter-selection procedures, and run-time or total-compute estimates are absent.

The quantile extension is largely heuristic: its residual is defined by a tautological subtraction and need not behave as a nonnegative regularizer, while the large-kappa and distributional assumptions used to obtain the squared-loss interpretation are not justified for the reported IQN setting. The IQN performance comparison therefore does not validate the categorical-loss theory.

strengths: The paper addresses an important open question—why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL—and proposes a potentially interesting perspective based on separating mean-related and distributional information.

The convex decomposition of a categorical target and the resulting linear decomposition of its cross-entropy loss are simple and clearly presented. The connection between categorical and histogram parameterizations is also useful pedagogically.
The empirical study spans value-based and actor–critic algorithms, Atari and MuJoCo environments, categorical and quantile critics, several random seeds, and an atom-count ablation.

The manuscript is generally well organized, situates itself relative to prior explanations of distributional RL, and acknowledges that its main analysis is limited to categorical methods. No material societal or human-subjects risks are apparent. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-36srawff/call-13ef3d0303b54ca88582a44ada6d1c68/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central exploration interpretation does not follow from the loss decomposition. Standard C51 minimizes the distributional critic loss but does not add f(H(mu,q)) to the actor reward or action-selection objective. The paper introduces this bonus in DERPI without deriving an equivalence to C51 or DSAC; f is arbitrary, and no gradient or policy-level identity connects DERPI to the evaluated algorithms.

Cross-entropy is not an uncertainty-mismatch measure: H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q) combines intrinsic target entropy with estimation error and remains H(mu) even when q=mu. Consequently, a large value need not mean that environmental uncertainty is underestimated. The analysis also does not separate aleatoric uncertainty from bootstrapping, approximation, or epistemic errors.

The main ablation is not diagnostic. H(mu,q) replaces the C51 target p with a modified target mu; decreasing the reported epsilon removes probability from the mean-containing bin and renormalizes the other bins. This generally changes the target expectation and Bellman fixed point and does not interpolate toward DQN or a mean-only learner—the mean component is precisely what is removed. Performance degradation under this increasingly distorted target therefore cannot establish that the proposed regularizer causes C51's advantage.

Several formal claims are incorrect or inadequately proved. Equation 39 establishes at most O(Delta), and generally Theta(Delta), rather than the claimed o(Delta). Proposition 6 proves only KL non-expansiveness and then incorrectly invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem, which requires a strict contraction. The DERPI result assumes a fixed q although q changes during distributional learning, drops the bonus term in its final optimality argument, and establishes at best policy iteration for a separately modified objective—not convergence of CDRL.

The histogram consistency theorem assumes i.i.d. return samples for a fixed state–action pair and does not justify a neural conditional categorical estimator trained from replay data. Its relationship to the fixed 51-atom experiments and nonlinear function approximation is therefore unclear.

The quantile extension is largely a tautological add-and-subtract decomposition. Its residual need not be a nonnegative regularizer, while the mean-loss approximation assumes both a large Huber threshold and P(y−Zbar<0)=1/2, which is generally false because a mean need not be a median.

The experiments do not directly measure visitation, return-distribution mismatch, or environmental uncertainty, so they cannot distinguish the proposed exploration mechanism from representation, optimization, or target-bias effects. Only eight selected Atari games with three seeds are used, there are no aggregate scores or significance tests, and one caption says seven MuJoCo environments while displaying eight.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the empirical claims. No code is supplied despite the checklist marking open access 'Yes' and promising release only after acceptance; Atari preprocessing and hyperparameters, categorical support bounds, network specifications, evaluation protocol, exact seeds, and sufficient compute/runtime information are missing or deferred to prior implementations.

strengths: The paper targets an important question—why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL—and the elementary cross-entropy decomposition provides a potentially useful lens. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xnwyyzsh/call-49d4ae4565d24177a4b9f7d59fffb79f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The presentation is generally organized, situates the question among distributional-RL and uncertainty-exploration literature, and includes extensive appendices.
The experiments span Atari and continuous-control environments, report multiple seeds with variability bands, and consider categorical and quantile critics.
The work presents no apparent material ethical concern; it uses standard simulated RL benchmarks and no human-subject or sensitive data.
weaknesses: The central conclusion does not follow from the decomposition. Equation (4) decomposes a critic-fitting loss, whereas Equations (7)–(9) introduce a new Bellman operator that explicitly rewards an arbitrary increasing function of cross-entropy. Standard C51/DSAC actors do not optimize this bonus. Consequently, the claimed intrinsic uncertainty-aware exploration mechanism is introduced rather than derived.

The cross-entropy H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q) is not an identified measure of environmental uncertainty: it conflates target entropy with estimation, optimization, projection, and model-mismatch errors. No result establishes that high cross-entropy means underestimated aleatoric uncertainty.

The principal ablation is not controlled. It replaces the original target p with mu rather than preserving the mean-related term and varying only the residual coefficient. From Equations (42)–(43), decreasing epsilon removes mass from the mean-containing bin and renormalizes the remaining bins, generally changing the target expectation and therefore the greedy policy. This procedure does not converge to DQN or SAC, so performance degradation cannot establish the causal importance claimed for the regularizer.

Several formal results contain concrete errors. Equation (39) establishes at best O(Delta), not o(Delta); weak convergence of shrinking uniform distributions to a Dirac mass does not imply that their probability of equaling the limiting point approaches one; and Proposition 6 proves only non-expansiveness, so invoking the Banach fixed-point theorem and uniqueness is invalid.

The policy-iteration result assumes a fixed q, and effectively a fixed auxiliary reward, while the practical critic and its target distribution evolve with the policy. Its proof also infers policy convergence merely from bounded monotone value functions, drops the entropy bonus in the final optimality condition, and only concerns optimality for the newly defined augmented objective—not the original MDP or ordinary distributional RL.

Proposition 3 compares only asymptotic global minimizers under very strong realizability and vanishing-bin assumptions. It does not justify equivalence at finite resolution or under nonlinear optimization, precisely where distributional RL's practical advantage is supposed to arise. The severe data-dependent validity condition is also underexplored; if the mean-containing bin has zero mass, only epsilon=1 is possible and the rescaled decomposition becomes singular.

The experiments measure returns but never demonstrate the proposed mechanism through visitation coverage, uncertainty calibration, cross-entropy/visitation correlations, or direct exploration diagnostics. Only eight Atari games with three seeds are shown, without an aggregate over the standard suite or significance tests, and the actor-critic ablation is largely insensitive to the decomposition parameter.

The mixed SAC/DSAC outcomes do not identify distinct exploration directions: architectural and critic-loss changes are confounded, and positive versus negative interactions are categorized post hoc. The unspecified transformation f from the theory is not implemented or tested.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript says code will be released only after acceptance while marking open access as “Yes”; the AC baseline description is circular; important support, preprocessing, evaluation, version, architecture, and compute-time details are absent or deferred to prior implementations.

The quantile extension is incomplete: its residual is defined tautologically as a difference of losses, may not be a regularizer, and its mean-loss approximation relies on unverified large-Huber-threshold and symmetry assumptions. Overall, these problems invalidate the main theoretical and empirical support rather than constituting minor correctable omissions.

strengths: The manuscript studies an important question—why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL—and proposes an intuitive decomposition of categorical cross-entropy into a mean-bin term and a residual distribution-matching term.

The paper is organized clearly, relates the proposed perspective to MaxEnt RL, and provides appendices containing proofs, implementation discussion, and an explicit limitation concerning generalization beyond categorical methods.
The empirical study covers eight Atari games and multiple MuJoCo tasks, reports variability over three or five seeds, and includes entropy, atom-count, and categorical/IQN comparisons.
The work presents no apparent material ethical risk.
weaknesses: The central exploration claim is not established. Decomposing a critic loss does not imply that the policy optimizes the cross-entropy as an augmented reward. The proposed DERPI operator inserts +f(H(mu,q)) into policy optimization, whereas the evaluated C51/DSAC algorithms merely use a distributional critic and do not implement this reward. Thus the theory analyzes a different, fixed-q algorithm from the experiments.

The decomposition is non-identifiable and does not cleanly separate expectation from higher-order uncertainty: epsilon is arbitrary, mu can retain first-moment information, and cross-entropy conflates target entropy with estimation mismatch. When the mean bin has zero mass, no nontrivial finite-alpha decomposition exists. Consequently, calling the residual an intrinsic aleatoric-uncertainty regularizer is insufficiently justified.

Several theoretical statements are incorrect. In Eq. 39, a bound of Delta/2 is O(Delta), not o(Delta); convergence in distribution of uniform shrinking bins does not imply probability one of exact equality for each finite Delta. KL non-expansiveness cannot support an application of Banach's fixed-point theorem, and the KL-to-Wasserstein claim omits compactness or moment assumptions. The policy-iteration proof also assumes fixed q, overlooks the policy dependence of the target-return distribution, and does not justify convergence of policies or optimality for the actual learning procedure.

The main epsilon ablation replaces the original target distribution with mu, redistributing or removing mass from the mean bin. Performance degradation under this increasingly distorted target does not isolate the benefit of a regularizer or constitute a controlled interpolation to DQN. Likewise, non-additive performance from combining SAC and distributional critics does not demonstrate distinct exploration directions. No visitation, uncertainty-calibration, or distribution-mismatch measurements directly test the claimed mechanism.

The empirical evidence relies largely on selected learning curves, with only three Atari seeds and no aggregate scores, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Alternative explanations such as representation, optimization, critic bias, and target distortion are not controlled.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the claims: code is only promised after acceptance, while exact network architectures, categorical support ranges, Atari preprocessing and training settings, evaluation protocol, seed details, and per-run or total compute are missing. The checklist's open-code and compute assertions therefore overstate what is supplied.

The quantile extension is largely heuristic: its residual decomposition is tautological, its quadratic approximation is not validated for the stated Huber setting, and it provides no rigorous bridge to the IQN experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL under nonlinear function approximation.

Subject to the validity condition on the mixture coefficient, the return-histogram decomposition and corresponding linear decomposition of cross-entropy are legitimate algebraic observations. Proposition 1 usefully states when the residual histogram is a valid density.
The study considers both Atari and continuous-control tasks, reports variability over multiple seeds, and includes ablations over the decomposition parameter, entropy variants, and atom counts.
The manuscript is broadly organized and engages relevant literature on distributional RL, exploration, and maximum-entropy RL. The work presents no apparent material research-ethics risk.
weaknesses: The central logical step is unsupported. Decomposing a critic training loss does not imply that the policy receives or maximizes an exploration bonus. Equations 7–9 introduce a new augmented reward involving an arbitrary increasing function of cross-entropy, but this reward is neither derived as an equivalent policy update nor used by standard C51 or DSAC. Those algorithms select actions using expected returns, not critic cross-entropy. Consequently, the fixed-q DERPI analysis does not establish an intrinsic exploration effect in the actual coupled algorithms.

The main ablation does not isolate the claimed regularizer. Replacing the original target p with the residual target mu and varying epsilon neither preserves the mean-related term nor interpolates to DQN. Even at the limiting setting, the method retains a categorical critic while removing and rescaling probability mass around the mean bin. Performance degradation can therefore result from increasingly distorted training targets rather than removal of uncertainty-aware exploration.

The uncertainty interpretation is problematic. The residual mu is not mean-free or exclusively higher-moment information; it depends on arbitrary binning and epsilon and generally retains mean information. Moreover, cross-entropy H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q) is not a discrepancy measure across state-action pairs: it can be large because mu itself has high entropy even when q=mu. The paper also conflates reducible estimation/TD error with irreducible environmental uncertainty.

Several theoretical claims contain substantive errors. Proposition 3 derives a bound of at most Delta/2 and then incorrectly labels it o(Delta), whereas it is generally Theta(Delta). Its probability-one statement also conflates convergence in distribution with equality for the finite-bin random variables. Proposition 6 proves at most non-expansiveness, so Banach's fixed-point theorem cannot be invoked to obtain uniqueness; its Wasserstein implication also omits necessary bounded-support or moment conditions. The DERPI proof only concerns a fixed auxiliary density and an augmented objective, drops the bonus in its purported optimality condition, and does not show that the policy sequence converges. None of this covers the practically relevant case where q changes jointly with the actor and critic.

The experiments do not directly measure the claimed mechanism: there are no state-visitation analyses, uncertainty-calibration measurements, cross-entropy trajectories, or demonstrations that policies preferentially visit underestimated states. Comparisons among AC, SAC, DAC, and DSAC show performance interactions but cannot establish distinct exploration directions. The Atari evaluation uses only eight selected games, with three seeds and no selection rationale, aggregate results, or significance testing.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The checklist claims open code access while stating only that code will be released after acceptance. The appendix omits important information such as complete Atari configurations, categorical support ranges, network architectures, preprocessing and evaluation protocols, software/environment versions, seed identities, and run times or total compute. Referring generally to RLKit and a prior DSAC implementation is insufficient for faithful reproduction.

The quantile extension is largely a tautological add-and-subtract decomposition. Its interpretation of the residual as a regularizer is not established, while the least-squares approximation assumes a large Huber threshold, approximate symmetry, and a 1/2 sign probability that need not hold for return distributions and do not match the stated practical threshold.

Overall, the sound portion is an elementary loss decomposition; the claimed novel contribution is the leap from that decomposition to intrinsic uncertainty-aware exploration. Because that leap is neither theoretically established nor experimentally identified, the main significance and originality claims are not supported.

strengths: The paper tackles an important, under-explored question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL. The proposed connection to uncertainty-guided exploration is potentially insightful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-4a4p30yz/call-2cde55ef2da5419ba9de89e4e5bb131d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The algebraic decomposition of categorical cross-entropy into a mean-bin term and a residual distribution-matching term is intuitive and presented with substantial supporting detail.
The experiments span Atari and MuJoCo, value-based and actor-critic methods, categorical and quantile critics, multiple atom counts, and several random seeds.
The manuscript is generally readable and well organized, provides an extensive appendix, and raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The central exploration interpretation is not established. Cross-entropy satisfies H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q), so a large value can reflect irreducible target entropy rather than estimation mismatch. Moreover, ordinary C51 selects actions through expected returns and does not maximize this cross-entropy as an exploration bonus.

Section 5 introduces a new Bellman objective that explicitly adds f(H(mu,q)) to the reward, but this is not shown to be equivalent to the C51 or DSAC algorithms evaluated experimentally. The convergence argument assumes a fixed q, whereas the critic changes throughout actual learning; thus it proves a standard result for a different, fixed-reward problem rather than the claimed behavior of distributional actor-critic.

The main ablation does not isolate the proposed regularization term. H(mu,q) replaces the original target distribution with mu. As the implementation parameter decreases, mass in the expectation-containing bin is removed and the remaining distribution is renormalized; this neither scales the residual term while retaining the mean term nor approaches a DQN target. Any degradation can therefore arise from changing and biasing the learning target, not from removing uncertainty-aware exploration.

The decomposition does not justify describing mu as information that 'excludes the expectation.' It is non-unique, depends on an arbitrary epsilon, generally retains mass in the expectation bin, and may change the distribution's mean. Consequently, labeling it purely as higher-moment or environmental-uncertainty information is unsupported.

Several theoretical claims are incorrect or incomplete. Equation 39 establishes at most O(Delta), not o(Delta); Proposition 6 derives non-expansiveness but then invokes the Banach fixed-point theorem, which requires strict contraction; and the policy-iteration proof omits key terms/conditions when asserting convergence and optimality. These are material because the paper presents theory as support for its central interpretation.

The experiments report only selected games, mostly three or five seeds, no aggregate metrics or significance tests, and no direct measurements of visitation, uncertainty calibration, or the proposed cross-entropy bonus. The SAC/DSAC comparisons confound the alleged exploration mechanism with critic parameterization and optimization. Reproducibility is also limited: no code is provided despite the checklist answering 'Yes,' the promised release is conditional on acceptance, and important implementation details are deferred to prior work. Overall, the interesting hypothesis is not yet supported by technically valid theory or causally diagnostic experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses an important open question—why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL—and proposes an intuitively appealing connection to uncertainty-aware exploration.
The categorical cross-entropy decomposition in Propositions 1–2 is a clear algebraic observation, subject to the required mixture-weight and support assumptions.
The evaluation spans value-based and actor-critic settings, several Atari and continuous-control environments, C51 and IQN critics, multiple seeds, and an atom-count ablation.
The manuscript is generally well organized, surveys relevant distributional-RL and exploration literature, provides appendices, and raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The central conceptual step is unsupported. A cross-entropy component of the critic-training loss does not become a positive reward bonus for the policy. DERPI explicitly inserts f(H(mu,q)) into a new Bellman operator, whereas standard C51/DSAC does not optimize this objective. The analysis furthermore freezes q, while q and the target distribution change during actual learning; the experiments do not implement DERPI or the proposed bonus.

H(mu,q) is not a clean measure of environmental uncertainty or even distributional mismatch: H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q), so it can be large when q=mu merely because mu has high entropy. Target-return variability also conflates environmental stochasticity, policy stochasticity, bootstrapping error, and estimation error. No direct exploration, visitation, or uncertainty measurements validate the claimed mechanism.

The principal epsilon ablation is not a valid interpolation from C51 to DQN. Replacing the Bellman target p by mu generally changes its mean; reducing epsilon increasingly removes mass from the mean-containing bin while retaining a full tail distribution. It never yields the scalar DQN target. The observed degradation can therefore be explained by progressively distorting the Bellman target rather than removing an uncertainty regularizer.

Several formal results contain substantive errors or gaps. Proposition 3 derives a bound of at most Delta/2 and incorrectly labels it o(Delta) rather than O(Delta), while also conflating empirical sampled targets with population Bellman targets. Proposition 6 proves only KL non-expansiveness and then incorrectly invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem. Its absolute-continuity and Wasserstein claims are incompletely stated. Theorem 1 does not justify policy convergence from value convergence, drops the bonus in a key optimality step, and applies only to an artificial fixed-bonus MDP. The quantile residual can be negative and its interpretation as a regularizer relies on unsupported approximations.

The experiments measure return but not the claimed exploration mechanism. The Atari evaluation uses only eight games and three seeds without a selection rationale or aggregate robust statistics; the continuous-control comparisons yield mixed results that are categorized post hoc as improvement or interference, without significance tests or controls for tuning and architectural effects.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the empirical claims. No code is supplied despite the checklist answering that open access is provided and then promising release only after acceptance. Important details such as categorical support ranges, Atari preprocessing and hyperparameters, full network architectures, evaluation protocol, software versions, hyperparameter-selection procedure, and per-run compute are missing.

The decomposition is non-unique and largely tautological—cross-entropy is linear in an arbitrarily chosen mixture of target distributions. Without a valid link to policy behavior or a causally identifying experiment, it does not establish the claimed intrinsic benefit of categorical distributional RL. The limitations section does not acknowledge these central restrictions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL under nonlinear function approximation.

The mixture decomposition of a categorical target into a mean-bin component and a residual distribution is simple and potentially useful as an analytical lens; Proposition 1 explicitly states its validity condition.

The manuscript is well organized and evaluates several algorithm families across Atari and MuJoCo, reporting multiple seeds and variability bands. The appendices provide substantial implementation and proof material.

The comparison with maximum-entropy RL raises interesting hypotheses about interactions between distributional critics and policy entropy. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent for these standard simulator experiments.
weaknesses: The central exploration claim does not follow from the analyzed algorithms. Standard C51 and distributional actor-critic methods do not add the cross-entropy H(mu,q) to the policy reward. Section 5 instead defines a new Bellman operator and DERPI objective containing this bonus, but establishes no equivalence between DERPI and C51/DSAC. Appendix J.4 effectively acknowledges that an algorithm jointly updating q and the policy remains undeveloped.

The decomposition is non-unique and may not exist in the claimed useful form. Its parameter can be chosen arbitrarily while the original loss remains unchanged, and validity requires epsilon >= 1-p_E. A categorical return can have zero mass in the bin containing its expectation, forcing epsilon=1, for which the finite mean term and alpha=epsilon/(1-epsilon) formulation break down. This substantially limits the purported general explanation of CDRL.

The main ablation does not isolate or weaken the proposed regularizer. H(mu,q) replaces the valid C51 target p with mu; as the plotted parameter decreases, mass is removed from the mean bin and the remaining tail mass is renormalized. This does not approach the DQN objective and can degrade performance simply by corrupting the target. Likewise, comparisons among AC, SAC, DAC, and DSAC do not demonstrate distinct exploration directions without measurements of visitation, uncertainty, or policy behavior.

Cross-entropy is treated as both a critic fitting loss and a policy entropy bonus. H(mu,q) is not purely a mismatch measure because it also contains H(mu), and target-current disagreement primarily reflects estimation/TD error rather than irreducible environmental uncertainty. Consequently, the terminology and uncertainty interpretation are not technically justified.

Several formal results contain substantive errors or omissions. Equation 39 proves at most O(Delta), not the claimed o(Delta). Appendix G invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem after establishing only non-expansiveness, which cannot imply a unique fixed point, and its Wasserstein implication needs bounded-support or moment assumptions. The policy-iteration proof also conflates convergence of bounded value sequences with convergence of policies and drops the bonus in its final optimality argument.

The empirical support is insufficient for the strength of the causal claims: only eight selected Atari games and three seeds are used, results are largely learning curves without aggregate statistics or significance tests, and some trends are non-monotone. The quantile extension is heuristic and depends on strong symmetry and large-Huber-threshold approximations.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says code will be released only after acceptance, gives limited Atari and architecture details, and reports merely that multiple RTX 3090 GPUs were used without run times or total compute. These central conceptual, theoretical, and experimental shortcomings outweigh the interesting motivation and require substantially more than a minor revision.

strengths: The paper targets an important, insufficiently understood question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL. Connecting this question to exploration and contrasting it with maximum-entropy RL is potentially useful.

The mixture identity for a categorical/histogram target and the resulting cross-entropy decomposition are simple and, under the stated feasibility condition, algebraically transparent. The paper also makes a useful effort to state assumptions, provide proofs, and acknowledge that its main analysis is limited to categorical methods.
The empirical effort spans value-based and actor-critic settings, multiple Atari and MuJoCo tasks, categorical and quantile critics, several random seeds, and an atom-count ablation.
The work poses little direct societal or human-subject risk, and no unresolved material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central interpretation does not follow from the decomposition. The split is non-unique because many values of the mixture coefficient produce different residual distributions. The residual can retain mean information and, when the mean-containing bin has zero probability, only the degenerate coefficient 1 is valid. Moreover, cross-entropy is not itself a discrepancy: H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q), so a large value can reflect irreducible target entropy rather than estimation error. Consequently, calling this term intrinsic uncertainty-matching regularization is not justified by the algebra.

The claimed exploration mechanism is not derived for C51 or DSAC. Standard distributional agents minimize the critic loss and choose actions using expected values; their actors do not receive the proposed positive reward f(H(mu,q)). Section 5 instead defines a new reward-shaped Bellman operator without proving it equivalent to the studied algorithms. Its convergence analysis fixes q, although q evolves in distributional RL, and treats the return-derived mu as fixed despite its policy dependence. Thus the theorem concerns an artificial shaped MDP, not intrinsic exploration by CDRL.

The main ablation does not isolate regularization strength. It replaces the valid C51 target p with mu; decreasing the reported epsilon removes probability from the mean bin and renormalizes the remaining bins. This increasingly distorts the Bellman target rather than interpolating from C51 to DQN or selectively removing higher-moment information. Degradation under this intervention therefore cannot establish that the proposed regularization causes C51's advantage.

There are concrete theoretical errors. Equation 39 derives an upper bound proportional to Delta and incorrectly labels it o(Delta) rather than O(Delta). Proposition 6 proves at most non-expansiveness in KL and then incorrectly invokes the Banach fixed-point theorem, which requires a strict contraction. The policy-iteration proof drops the bonus term at its purported fixed point and infers policy convergence from monotone value convergence without adequate justification. Several required absolute-continuity, bounded-support, and discount assumptions are also incomplete.

The quantile extension is largely heuristic. Its reduction to squared loss assumes, without general justification, that the mean of the target is also its median and that residuals lie in the quadratic Huber regime. The constructed residual need not be nonnegative, so interpreting it as regularization is unsupported.

The experiments never directly measure the proposed mechanism, such as state visitation, target-current distribution mismatch along visited trajectories, or behavior under controlled environmental stochasticity. The mixed SAC results only show ordinary interactions between critic and policy variants. Eight selected Atari games, three seeds, learning curves without aggregate scores or statistical tests, and post-hoc grouping of MuJoCo tasks are insufficient for the broad causal claims.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper supplies no code while marking open access as 'Yes' and promising release only after acceptance. Important details such as categorical support ranges, Atari preprocessing and evaluation protocol, full architectures, evaluation episode counts, and per-run/total compute are absent. The stated IQN quantile-fraction formula is also unclear or incorrect. The checklist's claim that no existing assets are used conflicts with reliance on RLKit, Atari, and MuJoCo.

Although the presentation is organized, it repeatedly conflates aleatoric return variability, epistemic estimation error, Bellman residual, entropy, and exploration. The limitations section acknowledges only the categorical scope and does not address the much more consequential gap between the proposed shaped objective and the actual algorithms. These central technical and empirical shortcomings outweigh the interesting motivation and experimental breadth.

strengths: The exact decomposition of a categorical target into a mean-bin component and a residual distribution is a potentially useful conceptual lens, and the paper attempts to connect distributional RL, label-smoothing-style regularization, and maximum-entropy RL.
The evaluation covers several Atari and MuJoCo environments, categorical and quantile-based critics, multiple seeds with standard-deviation bands, and an atom-count ablation.
The manuscript is generally organized, surveys relevant distributional-RL literature, supplies extensive appendices, and presents no material human-subject or societal-risk concern.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is not established by the algebra. The decomposition parameter is arbitrary and the residual distribution changes with it, so there is no uniquely identified intrinsic regularizer. Moreover, the residual is not purely information beyond the mean, and cross-entropy equals target entropy plus KL; its magnitude therefore does not directly measure estimator-target mismatch as repeatedly claimed.

The claimed exploration mechanism is absent from standard C51 and distributional SAC: their policies select actions using expected values, not the critic cross-entropy. The paper instead inserts an arbitrary increasing function of cross-entropy as a reward in DERPI, without deriving this objective from the actual algorithms, and DERPI itself is not evaluated.

Several theoretical statements or proofs are incorrect. Equation 39 establishes a distance of order Θ(Δ), not o(Δ); a non-expansive KL operator does not permit the claimed application of Banach's fixed-point theorem; the stated KL support condition is backwards; and the policy-iteration argument assumes a fixed critic while the practical critic and policy-dependent return target evolve jointly. The realizable, tabular/asymptotic analysis consequently does not address the nonlinear approximation regime motivating the paper.

The principal ablation is confounded. It replaces the original C51 target p with the residual μ rather than varying a regularizer while holding the mean objective fixed. At the low-ε endpoint, μ removes mass from the mean bin and does not reduce to DQN or a mean-only target; meanwhile, the full decomposition reconstructs exactly the same p for every valid decomposition parameter. Performance degradation under this target distortion therefore cannot identify the proposed regularization as C51's benefit.

The experiments do not measure exploration, state visitation, uncertainty calibration, or return-distribution mismatch. Results are mixed, use only three Atari or five MuJoCo seeds, lack aggregate scores and statistical tests, and the claimed mutual improvement/interference is a post-hoc description rather than evidence for distinct exploration directions.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the empirical claims: no code is supplied despite the checklist claiming open access based only on a future-release promise; important Atari settings, categorical support ranges, architecture details, task-selection criteria, and run-time requirements are missing. The limitations discussion does not acknowledge the central theoretical and experimental gaps.

strengths: The paper studies an important question—why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL—and the mean-bin/residual decomposition is intuitive and algebraically simple under its positivity condition. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-qwe189px/call-4fe4829963c64a348efb49aa30286796/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The evaluation spans value-based and actor–critic algorithms, Atari and continuous-control tasks, multiple seeds, categorical and quantile critics, and an atom-count ablation.
The manuscript is broadly organized and supplies appendices with proofs and implementation information. The simulated-benchmark study raises no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The central conceptual step is unsupported. Decomposing a critic's cross-entropy loss does not make its residual term an exploration reward in standard C51 or DSAC. The paper instead defines DERPI by explicitly inserting an arbitrary increasing function of that term into the reward, and proves results only for fixed q. It never establishes equivalence between DERPI and the practical algorithms evaluated.

The principal ablation does not isolate the claimed regularizer. Training only with H(μ,q) discards the mean-related term; ε=1 recovers C51, whereas ε approaching zero removes target mass from the mean bin and renormalizes the remaining distribution—it does not approach DQN or a classical mean-squared Bellman loss. Performance degradation can therefore be explained by increasingly distorted targets. Using both decomposed terms with their prescribed weights would merely reconstruct the original C51 objective.

Cross-entropy is incorrectly treated as a discrepancy and as evidence of underestimated environmental uncertainty. H(μ,q)=H(μ)+KL(μ||q), so it conflates target entropy with estimation mismatch; the bootstrapped return target also mixes aleatoric uncertainty, policy stochasticity, and approximation error. No theorem or diagnostic experiment connects this quantity to state visitation or exploration.

Several formal claims are incorrect or materially incomplete. Proposition 3 confuses weak convergence with exact point-mass probability, and its claimed o(Δ) rate is contradicted by its own Δ/2 bound, which is only O(Δ). Moreover, for a continuous target the validity constraint forces the mixture coefficient toward one as Δ shrinks, making the regularization weight diverge. Proposition 6 invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem after proving only non-expansiveness, states an incorrect support condition for finite KL, and omits conditions needed for Wasserstein convergence. The policy-iteration analysis excludes the changing critic and target distribution present in actual learning.

The experiments do not establish the proposed mechanism. Eight selected Atari games with three seeds, performance curves without aggregate statistics, and rankings among AC/SAC/DAC/DSAC cannot distinguish exploration from representation, optimization, target bias, or architectural effects. There are no controlled stochastic-versus-deterministic environments, visitation/coverage measurements, uncertainty calibration results, or evaluations of the proposed explicit bonus.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Despite marking open code access as “Yes,” the paper only promises release after acceptance. Essential details are absent, including categorical support ranges—especially consequential for MuJoCo—Atari preprocessing and exploration schedules, network sizes, evaluation protocol, seed values, and run-time/total-compute estimates. The quantile extension is also largely heuristic and does not repair the unsupported categorical exploration claim.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL under nonlinear function approximation.
The algebraic decomposition of a categorical target into a mean-bin component and a residual distribution is simple and potentially useful. Proposition 1 makes its validity condition explicit.
The experiments cover both Atari and MuJoCo, include value-based and actor-critic variants, report variability over multiple seeds, and include an atom-count ablation.
The manuscript is generally organized and supplies appendices with proofs and implementation details. The benchmark-based work raises no substantial ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central causal step is unsupported. In C51 or distributional SAC, cross-entropy is a critic-training loss; the acting policy does not maximize its magnitude. Section 5 instead inserts an arbitrary increasing function of H(μ,q) into the Bellman reward, thereby defining a new shaped-reward algorithm, DERPI. No equivalence to the original CDRL actor or greedy-policy update is proved, and the experiments do not implement this bonus. Consequently, the DERPI result cannot establish intrinsic exploration in CDRL.

Cross-entropy is not an uncertainty-discrepancy measure: H(μ,q)=H(μ)+KL(μ||q), so it can be large even when q=μ merely because the target has high entropy. The residual μ is also not mean-free, while prediction mismatch mixes environmental uncertainty with estimation, approximation, and optimization error. Thus the claimed aleatoric-uncertainty interpretation does not follow from the decomposition.

The principal ablation does not isolate the proposed regularizer. Replacing target p with μ and reducing ε deletes and renormalizes probability in the mean-containing bin; it neither interpolates toward DQN's scalar regression objective nor varies the residual weight while preserving the mean term. Performance degradation can therefore result simply from corrupting the categorical target. Likewise, comparisons among scalar/distributional critics and entropy/no-entropy actors contain architectural and optimization confounds.

Several theoretical statements are incorrect or incomplete. Proposition 3 derives an error bounded by Δ/2 but labels it o(Δ), although this is only O(Δ). Proposition 6 establishes at most KL non-expansiveness, so the invoked Banach fixed-point conclusion does not apply. DERPI has inconsistent discounting between its Bellman operator and stated objective, treats policy-dependent μ as fixed, drops the bonus in a key optimality step, and infers policy convergence from bounded monotone values without sufficient assumptions.

The experiments never directly measure exploration, state visitation, return-distribution mismatch, or uncertainty calibration. Learning curves on eight selected Atari games with three seeds and subsets of MuJoCo, without aggregate scores or statistical tests, cannot substantiate the proposed mechanism; the reported 'mutual improvement' and 'interference' are post-hoc interpretations of return curves.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the claims. The checklist marks code access as yes while promising release only after acceptance, and no code link is supplied. Important details such as Atari preprocessing and exploration schedules, C51 support bounds, complete network architectures, tuning procedures, and per-run or total compute are missing. The supplied document also exposes authors, affiliations, acknowledgements, and an arXiv identifier, contrary to double-blind submission requirements.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xbydq_h0/call-09649e7e3f374fbc87435ceffc4c83e3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important question: why distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL, and whether this relates to exploration.

Propositions 1–2 provide a simple algebraic decomposition of categorical cross-entropy under an explicit validity condition. The categorical/histogram correspondence and extensive appendices make the intended argument relatively easy to audit.
The evaluation spans value-based and actor–critic settings, Atari and MuJoCo, and includes seed variability, atom-count ablations, and comparisons involving policy entropy.
The paper is generally organized and readable, and the simulator-based study raises no material human-subject or societal-risk concern.
weaknesses: The central inference is unsupported. Decomposing H(p,q) into a mean-bin term and H(mu,q) does not make the latter an exploration reward in C51. C51 minimizes this target-fitting loss while selecting actions using expected return; it never maximizes H(mu,q). The paper instead defines a new Bellman operator that explicitly adds an arbitrary increasing function f(H) to reward. That constructed operator is not shown to be equivalent to C51, DSAC, or their gradients, so its policy-iteration result cannot establish the claimed intrinsic exploration mechanism.

Cross-entropy is incorrectly treated as a distributional discrepancy: H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q), so it can remain large when q=mu merely because the target has high entropy. It therefore does not specifically measure how far the current estimate “lags behind” the target. Moreover, the decomposition is non-canonical—many choices of epsilon and reference component yield different alleged bonuses for exactly the same original loss—undermining the claim that this is an intrinsic mechanism.

The main ablation does not isolate regularization strength. H(mu,q) replaces the valid C51 target p with a different target mu; lowering the reported epsilon removes/reweights probability at the mean-containing bin and generally changes the learned distribution and possibly its expectation. This procedure neither converges to DQN nor holds the Bellman target and mean-learning objective fixed. Its degradation can therefore be explained by increasingly distorting the target, rather than removing beneficial uncertainty-aware exploration.

Proposition 3 is not established in the stated stochastic setting. With repeated stochastic targets for a state-action pair, one-hot-bin cross-entropy learns a distribution over target bins, whereas squared-error FQI learns their conditional mean; realizability does not allow one output to equal incompatible samples. The proof also assumes that containing the full target implies closure under its decomposed component, and it explicitly concludes Delta/2=o(Delta), which is false: this is only O(Delta). At finite bin width, the uniform mean-bin component is centered at the bin midpoint, not necessarily at the target expectation.

The policy-iteration analysis fixes q even though q is jointly learned in the algorithms and appears to treat the policy-dependent return distribution mu as fixed during policy improvement. It proves, at most, standard policy iteration for a separately shaped reward—not convergence or optimality of practical distributional RL. Monotone convergence of values alone also does not prove convergence of policies under the stated assumptions.

Other theoretical errors further reduce confidence. In particular, KL non-expansiveness with factor 1 is not a strict contraction, so Banach’s fixed-point theorem cannot be invoked to infer a unique fixed point as done after Proposition 6. The quantile extension is largely an identity plus uncontrolled approximations; its residual can be negative and is not shown to be a regularizer.

The experiments never measure the proposed mechanism—state coverage, visitation of uncertain states, target/current KL, or correlation between the alleged bonus and action selection. Mixed SAC/DAC/DSAC performance cannot identify distinct exploration directions, and labeling environments post hoc as “mutual improvement” or “interference” is not an interaction analysis. The core Atari evidence uses only eight games and three seeds, with no aggregate score, confidence interval, or significance test.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims. No code accompanies the manuscript, although the checklist answers “Yes” to open access while promising release only after acceptance. Atari hyperparameters, software/environment versions, tuning and game-selection procedures, evaluation details, and per-run or total compute are incomplete. The checklist also incorrectly says that no existing assets are used despite reliance on Atari, MuJoCo, RLKit, and established implementations.

The limitations discussion mentions mainly extension beyond categorical RL but omits the consequential gaps between the analysis and practice: exact realizability, continuous Lipschitz densities and Delta-to-zero asymptotics versus finite categorical supports, fixed critics versus nonstationary neural learning, and the absence of a derived policy bonus. Because both the theoretical bridge and the causal empirical test underlying the headline claim fail, the deficiencies are fundamental rather than minor correctable issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL, particularly with nonlinear function approximation.

The return-density decomposition is a simple and potentially useful interpretive device, and the comparison with maximum-entropy RL highlights a conceptually interesting distinction between policy entropy and return-distribution information.
The empirical section covers value-based and actor-critic settings, Atari and continuous-control tasks, multiple distributional parameterizations, several ablations, and multiple random seeds.
The manuscript is generally organized and readable, provides substantial appendices, acknowledges its mainly categorical scope, and presents no apparent material ethical risk.
weaknesses: The central decomposition is non-unique and controlled by an arbitrary mixture coefficient. The residual density does not cleanly isolate higher moments or information 'beyond the expectation,' while a uniform distribution over the bin containing the mean does not preserve the exact mean at finite bin width. Moreover, the validity condition depends on the target's mean-bin probability, so the implementation induces target-dependent coefficients not covered by the fixed-alpha analysis.

The paper does not derive its claimed exploration mechanism from standard CDRL. It introduces a new Bellman operator that explicitly adds an arbitrary increasing function of cross-entropy as a reward, whereas C51 and the evaluated distributional actor-critic algorithms merely minimize a critic loss. Consequently, convergence of this constructed fixed-bonus policy iteration does not establish that ordinary CDRL performs such exploration.

Cross-entropy is incorrectly interpreted as distributional mismatch: H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q), so it can be large even when q exactly matches mu. Thus its magnitude does not by itself indicate that the current estimate 'lags far behind' the target, and the paper conflates environmental uncertainty with estimation error.

Several formal claims contain material gaps or errors. Proposition 3 establishes, at most, an idealized limiting-minimizer relationship rather than equivalence to finite-bin FQI; its displayed bound is O(Delta), generically Theta(Delta), not o(Delta). Proposition 6 proves only non-expansiveness under KL but then invokes fixed-point reasoning requiring contraction, with incomplete absolute-continuity and moment assumptions. DERPI fixes q even though q changes in the purported algorithm, leaves policy dependence of mu untreated, and assumes finite actions despite the continuous-action experiments.

The principal ablation does not isolate the proposed regularizer. The decomposition yields a mean-bin loss plus a weighted residual loss, but the experiments replace the original target by mu and optimize H(mu,q) alone. Decreasing the implementation ratio removes mass from the mean bin and changes the target distribution; it does not continuously recover DQN or selectively reduce a residual regularization coefficient. Therefore, the observed performance trends do not causally validate the proposed explanation.

There is no direct evidence of exploration: no state-coverage, visitation, return-entropy, target-current KL, or uncertainty-calibration measurements are reported. Performance differences can equally arise from representation, optimization, target distortion, or critic-bias effects already associated with categorical losses.

The evaluation uses only eight selected Atari games with three seeds, lacks suite-level aggregate metrics or significance tests, and exhibits mixed or weakly monotonic trends, especially in the actor-critic ablation. The MaxEnt interaction experiments also change several algorithmic components and cannot establish distinct exploration directions from learning curves alone.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the claims: code is promised only after acceptance, Atari hyperparameters and evaluation protocols are missing, and crucial details such as categorical support ranges, network architecture, library versions, and exact compute/runtime are deferred to prior implementations. The checklist's claims of open code and no use of existing assets are inconsistent with the manuscript.

The limitations discussion omits the most consequential restrictions: the arbitrary decomposition, asymptotic and realizability assumptions, fixed-critic analysis, absence of a link to the implemented algorithms, and inability of the experiments to distinguish exploration from optimization effects.

strengths: The paper addresses an important open question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL. Connecting distributional losses, exploration, and maximum-entropy RL is potentially valuable.

Proposition 2 gives a simple algebraic decomposition of categorical cross-entropy into a mean-bin term and a residual distribution-matching term, with an explicit validity condition for the constructed residual density.
The empirical study spans Atari and continuous-control tasks, includes C51- and IQN-based critics, varies the decomposition parameter and atom count, and reports variability over multiple seeds.

The presentation is generally organized, relevant distributional-RL and exploration literature is discussed, and the work appears to pose no material human-subject, privacy, or other research-ethics risk.
weaknesses: The central exploration claim does not follow from the loss decomposition. Proposition 2 only rewrites the critic loss; standard C51 and DSAC policies select actions using expected returns and do not receive the proposed f(H(mu,q)) bonus. Section 5 introduces a new Bellman operator containing that bonus by definition, without proving equivalence to the evaluated algorithms. Thus DERPI does not explain the claimed intrinsic behavior of C51 or DSAC.

The decomposition becomes degenerate in the asymptotic regime used to connect it to FQI. Validity requires epsilon >= 1-p_E; for a continuous density, p_E is typically O(Delta), so Delta -> 0 forces epsilon -> 1 and alpha=epsilon/(1-epsilon) to diverge. If a multimodal distribution has zero mass in the bin containing its mean, no finite nontrivial decomposition exists. Moreover, the single-bin uniform component identifies only a mean-containing bin, not the exact mean.

Several formal results contain substantive errors. Proposition 3 does not establish equivalence between classification of sample-dependent target-mean bins and squared Bellman regression under stochastic rewards or transitions, and its claimed rate is incorrect because Delta/2 is O(Delta), not o(Delta). Appendix G invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem after proving only non-expansiveness, not contraction. Theorem 1 treats q as fixed, does not cover actual joint actor-critic learning, drops the entropy bonus in its optimality step, and at most concerns the artificially shaped objective rather than the original MDP return.

Cross-entropy is misinterpreted as a discrepancy: H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q). Across state-action pairs, a large value can result from high target entropy, estimator mismatch, or both. Consequently it does not by itself show that environmental uncertainty is underestimated, and the paper conflates aleatoric environmental uncertainty with epistemic approximation error.

The main epsilon ablation does not isolate the proposed regularizer. The experiments replace the complete target p with mu instead of retaining the mean term and varying the residual coefficient. Decreasing the implemented epsilon removes mass from the mean bin and renormalizes off-mean mass; it does not approach the DQN objective. Performance degradation can therefore arise from increasingly distorted training targets rather than loss of an exploration benefit.

No experiment directly tests the proposed mechanism: there are no measurements of state visitation versus cross-entropy, return-distribution mismatch, uncertainty calibration, or exploration in controlled stochastic MDPs. Comparisons among AC, SAC, DAC, and DSAC show task-dependent architectural performance differences, but do not establish distinct exploration directions. The Atari evidence is limited to eight games and three seeds, with no standard 57-game aggregate or statistical tests.

The quantile extension is heuristic. Its residual is a tautological difference that need not be nonnegative or act as a regularizer, while the mean-loss approximation assumes large Huber threshold and roughly symmetric residuals. These assumptions are neither justified nor aligned with the stated IQN configuration.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the empirical claims. Code is not available despite the checklist marking open access as 'Yes' and only promising release after acceptance. Exact Atari settings, network specifications, categorical support ranges, software versions, seeds, and run times are missing; compute reporting is limited to 'multiple RTX 3090 GPUs.' Existing benchmark assets and their licenses are also incorrectly marked as not applicable.

The algebraic split is non-unique and comparatively elementary, and the work supplies neither a new practical algorithm nor a valid performance or sample-complexity guarantee. Because the novel contribution is primarily the exploration interpretation, the unsupported theory-to-algorithm link substantially limits originality and significance.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important question—why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL—and offers a potentially interesting connection to exploration and maximum-entropy RL. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-1s5p2aad/call-ed3f02fb2b204923a7bfa38c7c06a585/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The mixture decomposition of a categorical target into a mean-bin component and a residual distribution is simple and clearly presented, including a validity condition and extensive appendices.

The empirical study spans Atari and MuJoCo, reports variability over three or five seeds, and includes ablations over the decomposition parameter, atom count, categorical critics, and quantile critics.

The paper is generally well organized, engages with relevant distributional-RL literature, acknowledges that the main analysis is specific to categorical losses, and raises no material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central decomposition does not identify an intrinsic regularizer uniquely. For any admissible epsilon, the same target distribution admits a different split, and at epsilon=1 the entire C51 loss is labeled the residual term. Moreover, the residual distribution need not isolate higher moments: it can have a different mean, and both terms affect all learned probabilities through normalization. Thus the algebra alone does not establish a distinct causal mechanism behind CDRL's benefits.

Cross-entropy H(mu,q) is incorrectly treated as a discrepancy or uncertainty-estimation error. It equals H(mu)+KL(mu||q), so it can be large even when q=mu merely because the target has high entropy. Consequently, the proposed increasing reward f(H(mu,q)) does not specifically reward states where the estimate “lags behind” the target.

There is a major gap between CDRL and the actor-critic theory. Standard C51 chooses actions using expected returns, and a standard distributional actor maximizes its critic's expected value; neither adds the critic cross-entropy as a reward bonus. Equations 7–9 instead postulate a new augmented Bellman operator. The DERPI result assumes a fixed q and arbitrary bounded f, whereas q changes during actual distributional learning. Therefore it proves a routine policy-iteration fact for a different augmented MDP, not the claimed implicit exploration behavior of C51 or DSAC.

The main ablation is confounded. Replacing the C51 target p by mu and lowering the plotted parameter removes probability from the mean-containing bin and renormalizes the remaining bins; it neither continuously removes distributional information nor approaches a DQN squared-error target. It also changes the target expectation. Performance degradation under this increasingly altered target therefore cannot establish that uncertainty-aware regularization causes C51's advantage.

The experiments never measure the claimed mechanism—cross-entropy/KL mismatch, environmental uncertainty, visitation of uncertain states, or exploratory behavior. The AC/SAC/DAC/DSAC comparisons change critic representation and objectives simultaneously, and the “mutual improvement” versus “interference” grouping is descriptive and post hoc. Only selected Atari games are reported, with three seeds and no aggregate Atari metric or statistical testing.

Several mathematical statements are incorrect or insufficiently justified. Equation 39 concludes Delta/2=o(Delta), although it is only O(Delta). Proposition 6 establishes at most non-expansiveness in KL but invokes the Banach fixed-point theorem, which requires a strict contraction. Theorem 1 infers policy convergence from bounded monotone values without adequate conditions and its limiting optimality argument omits the regularization term. The histogram consistency result also concerns an i.i.d. empirical histogram under a Lipschitz density, not a neural C51 estimator and often not discrete-return environments such as Atari.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the checklist claims open code while saying it will only be released after acceptance, and the manuscript lacks important details such as Atari preprocessing/evaluation protocol, categorical support ranges, task-selection rationale, hyperparameter-selection procedures, and per-run or total compute. These issues, together with the unsupported causal interpretation and proof errors, outweigh the paper's interesting hypothesis.

strengths: The paper addresses an important open question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL, and the proposed comparison with maximum-entropy exploration is potentially interesting.
The cross-entropy decomposition is algebraically transparent under its stated validity condition, and the manuscript attempts to connect value-based and actor-critic settings.
The evaluation spans several Atari and continuous-control tasks, multiple seeds, categorical and quantile critics, and an atom-count ablation.

The paper is organized and readable, provides extensive appendices, and raises no material ethical concerns. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-du0imnh_/call-6b732d1064324be3bb9a151137c353bd/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central claimed mechanism is not derived. C51/DSAC minimizes cross-entropy in the critic while actions or actors use the expected return. The paper instead defines a new Bellman operator containing +f(H) as a reward bonus, without proving that standard C51 or DSAC implements this operator. DERPI is neither equivalent to nor evaluated as the algorithms used experimentally.

Cross-entropy is not a measure of distributional mismatch: H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q). It can therefore be large when q=mu merely because the target is diffuse. Rewarding it may favor intrinsically noisy states rather than states whose estimates 'lag behind.' Return dispersion also conflates aleatoric, policy-induced, and estimation uncertainty.

The decomposition is non-unique and controlled by an arbitrary epsilon; analogous decompositions can use other bins. The induced mu is not mathematically isolated 'higher-moment information beyond the mean,' and rewriting an unchanged loss does not itself establish a new regularization or exploration effect.

The main ablation does not vary the weight of the decomposed regularizer while retaining the decomposed objective. It replaces the original target p with mu and discards the mean-related term. As epsilon approaches zero, this removes and renormalizes mass in the mean-containing bin; it does not approach DQN/SAC and generally changes the target expectation. Consequently, the observed performance interpolation is heavily confounded.

Several theoretical results contain substantive errors or missing assumptions. Proposition 3 assumes that a class containing the target distribution also contains its single-bin component, which does not follow. Equation (39) establishes Theta(Delta), not the claimed o(Delta). Appendix G invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem after showing only non-expansiveness. The DERPI argument fixes a critic unlike the practical algorithm, may use a policy-dependent bonus, omits the bonus in its concluding greedy condition, and does not prove policy convergence from bounded monotone values.

The experiments do not directly measure uncertainty, cross-entropy mismatch, state visitation, or exploration. Comparing AC/SAC/DAC/DSAC performance, then grouping tasks post hoc as 'improvement' or 'interference,' cannot establish distinct exploration directions. Atari results use only three seeds and lack aggregate scores or significance tests.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the checklist claiming otherwise: code is only promised after acceptance, and essential details such as Atari preprocessing and evaluation protocol, categorical support ranges, complete architectures and hyperparameters, software versions, and run-level compute are absent.

The quantile extension is largely heuristic: its residual is defined tautologically, it assumes the mean acts as a median via P(y-barZ<0)=1/2, and it relies on an unspecified large-Huber-threshold approximation. The limitations section does not acknowledge these issues or the core disconnect between the proposed bonus and actual distributional RL.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important question—why distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL—and offers a potentially interesting uncertainty-oriented perspective. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-i6ped2n4/call-dd16bda3b38a4ae3975e04e3973e991b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

For a fixed target and admissible decomposition parameter, the categorical cross-entropy identity separating a mean-bin term from a residual distribution-matching term is transparent and may be a useful analytical lens.

The evaluation covers value-based and actor-critic algorithms, Atari and MuJoCo tasks, categorical and quantile critics, and atom-count ablations. Seed variability is shown, the paper is generally organized, and no material human-subject or dual-use concern arises.
weaknesses: The central exploration claim is not established. Standard C51 and distributional SAC do not add the critic cross-entropy to the policy reward; the paper introduces a new Bellman operator and DERPI update that explicitly do so, then interprets this constructed algorithm as an intrinsic property of the standard algorithms. No equivalence between their actual policy updates is proved.

Cross-entropy is not the claimed estimation-discrepancy measure: H(μ,q)=H(μ)+KL(μ||q), so it can remain large when q=μ merely because the target has high entropy. Moreover, μ depends on an arbitrary decomposition parameter and does not cleanly represent information 'beyond the mean.' The validity constraint is state-dependent and can force ε=1 when the mean bin has zero mass, making the rescaled coefficient undefined.

Several formal results contain substantive errors or gaps. Equation 39 concludes Δ/2=o(Δ), although the displayed distance is Θ(Δ). Appendix G invokes Banach's fixed-point theorem from non-expansiveness rather than a strict contraction. The policy-iteration result assumes a fixed q, does not cover joint critic-policy learning, and its proof does not establish the stated optimality for the actual distributional algorithm. The quantile extension relies on an unjustified symmetry assumption and defines its residual largely tautologically.

The main ablation does not isolate the alleged regularizer. Replacing target p by μ and varying the parameter redistributes probability away from the mean bin and generally changes the target expectation; it is not equivalent to scaling the residual term while retaining the mean-related objective, nor does its endpoint recover DQN/SAC. Performance degradation can therefore result from biased targets. There are also no direct measurements of state coverage, aleatoric uncertainty, distributional mismatch, or exploration behavior.

The empirical evidence is insufficient for the breadth and causality of the claims: only selected games are used, Atari results have three seeds, there are no aggregate scores or significance tests, and the 'mutual improvement/interference' conclusions are post-hoc readings of curves. Reproducibility is also incomplete: no code is supplied despite the checklist answering yes, crucial Atari/support/network/evaluation details are missing, and compute reporting gives neither run time nor GPU count. The limitations section does not acknowledge these restrictions or the fixed-q and asymptotic assumptions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important open question—why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL—and proposes an intuitive histogram-loss decomposition. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-t0f1r61o/call-5466e25381f548b59693ea99374e77b8/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical study spans Atari and MuJoCo, includes C51- and IQN-based critics, varies atom counts, and reports variability across three or five seeds.
The manuscript is generally well organized, surveys relevant distributional-RL and exploration literature, and provides proofs and implementation details in an extensive appendix.
The work uses standard simulated benchmarks and presents no apparent material ethical risk.
weaknesses: The central exploration claim does not follow from the loss decomposition. Standard C51 and the evaluated distributional actor-critic select actions using expected returns; they do not add cross-entropy to the policy reward. Equations 7–9 explicitly introduce a different shaped-reward algorithm, DERPI, without proving equivalence to C51 or DSAC.

The decomposition is non-unique because epsilon is arbitrary, so algebraically labeling one component a regularizer cannot identify a causal mechanism. Moreover, H(mu,q)=H(mu)+KL(mu||q): its magnitude is not purely distribution mismatch, remains large for uncertain targets even when q=mu, and does not distinguish under- from over-dispersion.

The main ablation does not isolate the proposed regularizer. H(mu,q) replaces the Bellman target by the residual distribution mu; as the displayed epsilon approaches zero, probability is removed from the mean-containing bin and redistributed elsewhere. This neither approaches DQN nor preserves the target expectation in general, so degradation can result from biased Bellman targets rather than loss of uncertainty-aware exploration.

The experiments never manipulate environmental stochasticity or directly measure uncertainty calibration, state-action coverage, visitation, or exploration. Factorial comparisons among AC, SAC, DAC, and DSAC therefore support only environment-dependent performance differences, not the claimed mechanism. Several apparent differences also lack statistical testing and use only three Atari seeds.

There are substantive proof errors. Proposition 3 derives a bound of at most Delta/2 and then calls it o(Delta), although it is only O(Delta) and the ratio need not vanish. Appendix G proves only KL non-expansiveness with factor one but invokes the Banach fixed-point theorem, which requires contraction. Theorem 2 is also used outside its stated continuous-density/sample-asymptotic setting.

The DERPI result assumes a fixed critic distribution while the practical target distribution changes with the policy; its proof does not establish convergence of the policy sequence or optimality for the original unregularized MDP. It also concerns finite actions, whereas the supporting MuJoCo experiments use continuous actions.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is promised only after acceptance, Atari settings and several architectural/evaluation details are missing, and compute reporting gives neither run time nor total usage. The checklist also marks existing assets as inapplicable despite reliance on RLKit, Atari, and MuJoCo.
